edges.description: Successful neuroinvasion delivers virus to CNS-resident neurons, where viral replication begins.
Infected and bystander CNS-resident cells mount cell-intrinsic type I/III interferon responses to restrict viral replication.
Neuronal infection triggers innate immune sensing and recruitment of an inflammatory response within the brain.

When neuron-intrinsic interferon defense fails to contain the virus (notably with inborn errors of the TLR3-interferon axis), unchecked neuronal viral replication amplifies innate immune sensing and the neuroinflammatory response.
Sustained neuroinflammation, blood-brain barrier breakdown, and immune cytotoxicity combine with direct viral injury to damage brain parenchyma and produce edema.
Widespread parenchymal injury and edema disrupt cortical function, producing altered mental status and encephalopathy.
Parenchymal injury, inflammation, and blood-brain barrier disruption lower the seizure threshold and drive acute symptomatic seizures and epileptogenesis.
Focal parenchymal damage (e.g., temporal lobe involvement in HSV) produces focal neurologic signs such as aphasia and hemiparesis.

Lytic neuronal injury and antigen release during acute HSV-1 infection can prime a secondary autoimmune response against neuronal surface antigens, most often the NMDA receptor, in a substantial minority of patients.

Post-HSE autoimmune encephalitis produces a second phase of neurological worsening (decreased consciousness, choreoathetosis, or new psychiatric symptoms) that can be mistaken for HSV relapse but reflects an antibody-mediated rather than infectious process.

nodes.description: Altered mental status / encephalopathy ranging from confusion and behavioral change to reduced consciousness and coma.

evidence.reference_title: Can we forecast poor outcome in herpes simplex and varicella zoster encephalitis? A narrative review.
evidence.snippet: Herpes simplex virus (HSV) and varicella zoster virus (VZV) are among the most commonly diagnosed infectious causes of sporadic encephalitis worldwide.

nodes.description: Neuronal infection elicits a host inflammatory response with microglial and astrocytic activation and a cytokine/chemokine surge (e.g., IL-6, IL-8, IL-1, TNF, CXCL1, CCL2). This neuroinflammation, together with T-cell-mediated immunity, both restricts viral entry into the CNS and contributes to immunopathology and blood-brain barrier breakdown.

evidence.reference_title: The immunobiology of herpes simplex virus encephalitis and post-viral autoimmunity.
evidence.snippet: Herein, we review the latest evidence behind the phenotypic progression and underlying immunobiology of HSE including the cytokine/chemokine environment, the role of pathogen-recognition receptors, T- and B-cell immunity and relevant inborn errors of immunity.

evidence.reference_title: T Cells in Tick-Borne Flavivirus Encephalitis: A Review of Current Paradigms in Protection and Disease Pathology.
evidence.snippet: With access to neural tissues despite the selectively permeable blood-brain barrier, T cells have emerged as one notable contributor to neuroinflammation.

nodes.description: CNS-resident neurons restrict neurotropic viruses through cell-intrinsic antiviral immunity, prominently the TLR3-dependent induction of type I and type III interferons and downstream interferon-stimulated genes, as well as interferon-independent intrinsic mechanisms. Inborn errors that disrupt these neuron-intrinsic pathways (see Genetic section) underlie a substantial fraction of childhood herpes simplex encephalitis by permitting unchecked HSV-1 replication in the brain.

evidence.reference_title: Genetic defects of brain immunity in childhood herpes simplex encephalitis.
evidence.snippet: In this Review, we examine essential cellular and molecular mechanisms of cell-intrinsic antiviral immunity in the brain that are disrupted in individuals with HSE.

evidence.reference_title: Inborn Errors of Immunity Predisposing to Herpes Simplex Virus Infections of the Central Nervous System.
evidence.snippet: Previous studies have uncovered defects in the innate Toll-like receptor 3 pathway and production of type I interferon (IFN-I) in children and adults that predispose them to herpes simplex encephalitis.

nodes.description: Once in the CNS, neurotropic viruses replicate within neurons (and other CNS-resident cells), producing direct viral cytotoxicity. Cortical neurons underlie forebrain infection while brainstem neurons underlie brainstem infection, and cell-intrinsic antiviral immunity in these neurons is the critical determinant of whether infection is contained.

evidence.reference_title: Genetic defects of brain immunity in childhood herpes simplex encephalitis.
evidence.snippet: They operate in cortical or brainstem neurons, and underlie forebrain and brainstem infections, respectively.

nodes.description: Direct viral cytotoxicity, excitotoxicity, cytokine-mediated injury, and immune-mediated damage produce neuronal loss, gliosis, perivascular cuffing, demyelination, and cerebral edema. This tissue damage is the substrate for the clinical encephalopathy and is associated with the permanent neurologic sequelae seen in survivors.

evidence.reference_title: Neuropathogenesis of Encephalitic Alphaviruses in Non-Human Primate and Mouse Models of Infection.
evidence.snippet: survivors of infection often suffer from permanent neurological sequelae as a result of sustained neuroinflammation and neurological insults encountered.

nodes.description: In roughly a quarter of patients, herpes simplex encephalitis (HSE) is followed by a distinct secondary autoimmune encephalitis mediated by antibodies against neuronal cell-surface and synaptic antigens, most commonly the NMDA receptor, arising weeks after the acute infection. This chronic complication is immunologically and clinically distinct from ongoing viral disease: it does not respond to antiviral therapy and instead requires immunotherapy (corticosteroids, plasma exchange, or rituximab). Presentation is age-dependent, with choreoathetosis and decreased consciousness predominating in young children and psychosis predominating in older children and adults.

evidence.reference_title: Frequency, symptoms, risk factors, and outcomes of autoimmune encephalitis after herpes simplex encephalitis: a prospective observational study and retrospective analysis.
evidence.snippet: during follow-up, 14 (27%) patients developed autoimmune encephalitis and all 14 (100%) had neuronal antibodies (nine [64%] had NMDA receptor [NMDAR] antibodies and five [36%] had other antibodies) at or before onset of symptoms.

evidence.reference_title: Herpes Simplex Virus-1 Encephalitis in Adults: Pathophysiology, Diagnosis, and Management.
evidence.snippet: chronic complications, including the development of autoimmune encephalitis associated with antibodies to the N-methyl-D-aspartate receptor and other neuronal cell surface and synaptic epitopes.

nodes.description: Seizures are a common presenting symptom of viral CNS infection and may occur acutely or as later spontaneous seizures (acquired epilepsy).

evidence.reference_title: Molecular Mechanisms in the Genesis of Seizures and Epilepsy Associated With Viral Infection.
evidence.snippet: Seizures are a common presenting symptom during viral infections of the central nervous system (CNS) and can occur during the initial phase of infection ("early" or acute symptomatic seizures), after recovery ("late" or spontaneous seizures, indicating the development of acquired epilepsy), or both.

nodes.description: Neurotropic viruses reach the central nervous system either by hematogenous spread across the blood-brain barrier or by retrograde axonal transport along peripheral nerves (e.g., trans-synaptic spread of HSV-1 from the trigeminal or olfactory pathways). This neuroinvasion establishes infection of brain parenchyma and is the initiating event of viral encephalitis.

evidence.reference_title: Advances in viral encephalitis: Viral transmission, host immunity, and experimental animal models.
evidence.snippet: Neurotropic virus infection-induced viral encephalitis (VE), especially the symptomatic inflammation of the meninges and brain parenchyma, has attracted growing attention due to its high mortality and disability rates.
